newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-FRENCH QUARTER-FINAL HAS UNFAMILIAR LOOK.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-FRENCH QUARTER-FINAL HAS UNFAMILIAR LOOK.

text.p: While the French Open women's final is shaping up as a battle between Martina Hingis and Steffi Graf, two of tennis's most recognisable names, the men's title could well be a tussle between players few have ever heard of.

As the French Open began its second week on Monday only two seeded players, defending champion Yevgeny Kafelnikov and twice winner Sergi Bruguera, had survived to make it through to the quarter-finals, the fewest in any grand slam tournament in the Open era.
The other six coveted spots are occupied by less familiar names such as Galo Blanco, Filip Dewulf, Gustavo Kuerten and Hicham Arazi.

Blanco, ranked 111 and perhaps the least likely of the 34 Spaniards who began the tournament to have a chance of appearing in the final, remains in the hunt while the rest of his compatriots, with the exception of Bruguera, have fallen by the wayside.
Bruguera, winner of the title in 1993 and 1994, earned his fourth quarter-final appearance in five years with a tense four-set victory over 1989 winner and second seed Michael Chang.

He will now meet Hicham Arazi, ranked 55th in the world, who upset the mercurial seventh seed Marcelo Rios of Chile in five sets, becoming the first Moroccan to reach the quarter-finals of a grand slam event.
"If he plays as well as he did against me he will kill Bruguera," said Rios.

"Maybe these players are anonymous for you but not me, I know them very well," said Bruguera, the 16th seed. "It is truth that I was surprised when players like Alex Corretja and Aberto Costa lost because I thought they had a really good draw.
"I think I'm playing better because I'm hungry for victories. I want so much to win."

Blanco, who made a first round exit in his only other effort at Roland Garros, has enjoyed good luck as much as fine form, advancing through his quarter of the draw, which contained Goran Ivanisevic, Richard Krajicek, Albert Costa and Wayne Ferreira, without meeting a seeded player.

The 20-year-old Spaniard secured his place in the final eight with a win over 1992 finalist Petr Korda. He will now take on Australia's Patrick Rafter, ranked 25 in the world, who reached his first grand slam quarter-final after a four-set success over compatriot Mark Woodforde.
"I prefer not to think about the future," said Blanco. "I work hard. I go on to the court I know I can win, I know I can lose, I know I can fight.
"In the quarter-finals I will go onto the court and give everything I have. I will fight, I will go to the end."
Kafelnikov, who had said it would take a miracle to retain his title, now must feel it a distinct possibility with all the players left in his half of the draw ranked outside the top 50.

Next up for the third-seeded Russian is 20-year-old Gustavo Kuerten, ranked 66 in the world. Kitted out from head-to-toe in yellow and blue, he became the first Brazilian in 29 years to reach the quarter-finals when he survived a five set duel over Andrei Medvedev that took two days to complete because of bad light.
"I think now in the quarter-finals, anything can happen," said Kuerten, who lists 1995 champion Thomas Muster among his earlier victims. "I'm playing pretty well but so is Kafelnikov.
"I played him once before in Stuttgart last year and lost but I'm playing much better now.
In a line-up of unlikely quarter-finalists, however, it is Belgium qualifier Filip Dewulf who's stands out most.

Dewulf, ranked 122 in the world will take on number 65 Magnus Norman of Sweden, who probably had the toughest road to the final eight having knocked aside world number one Pete Sampras and 15th seed Marc Rosset along his way.
Quarter-final lineup:
16-Sergi Bruguera (Spain) v Hicham Arazi (Morocco)
Galo Blanco (Spain) v Patrick Rafter (Australia)
3-Yevgeny Kafelnikov (Russia) v Gustavo Kuerten (Brazil)
Filip Dewulf (Belgium) v Magnus Norman (Sweden)
